findings.title: Uniform card styling
findings.summary: 4 of 4 card-like elements all use the exact same 'rounded-2xl shadow-lg' combination
findings.why: When every card carries an identical corner radius and drop shadow, nothing sits forward or back, so the page reads flat no matter how much is on it. This pattern is commonly associated with an accepted default rather than a chosen one.
findings.fix: Give one tier of card a heavier surface — a stronger border or a lifted background — and let the rest sit quieter.

findings.title: Numbered step/feature labels
findings.summary: Found 3 short numbered labels (01, 02, 03) — a common auto-generated 'step/feature' eyebrow pattern
findings.why: Numbering every section is a layout habit that fills space without deciding what matters. Readers skip it, and it is one of the more recognisable generated-page tells.
findings.fix: Drop the numbers. If the order genuinely matters, say so in the heading itself.

findings.title: Generic marketing phrasing
findings.summary: 9 instance(s) of generic marketing phrasing found in headings/copy
findings.why: These verbs describe no product in particular, which is why they turn up everywhere. A reader learns nothing from them, and a model reading the page has nothing specific it could repeat back about you.
findings.fix: Replace each with the specific thing it does, in your own words. If a sentence would be true of any company, it is not saying anything.

findings.title: Unmodified default colors
findings.summary: 3 colors on the page are unmodified defaults from common component libraries/page builders
findings.why: Framework defaults are recognisable precisely because nobody changed them. It is the quickest signal that a theme was accepted rather than chosen.
findings.fix: Shift the hue and lightness away from the default, even slightly. A 10–15 degree hue rotation is usually enough to stop it reading as stock.

findings.title: Flat heading hierarchy
findings.summary: 9 of 9 headings are all <h3> — little real heading hierarchy despite repeated sections
findings.why: A hierarchy that barely changes gives a reader nothing to land on. The eye needs a clear first stop, and a crawler needs to know which heading owns which block of text.
findings.fix: Widen the gap: one h1, real h2s for sections, h3s inside them. Cut a level if you are carrying four.

findings.title: Overused icon set
findings.summary: 4 uses of icons commonly overused in generated UI (sparkles, arrow-right, zap, check-circle)
findings.why: The same handful of glyphs carry most generated pages. They are not wrong, they are invisible from familiarity.
findings.fix: Keep them where they earn it, but let at least one visual on the page be specific to you.

findings.title: H1 count
findings.summary: The page has no h1
findings.why: The h1 is the one heading that says what this page is. Without it both a reader skimming and a crawler indexing have to infer it from context.
findings.fix: Promote the main headline to an h1. There should be exactly one.

findings.title: Thin page
findings.summary: Only 98 words of body copy on this page
findings.why: A page this short rarely answers the question that brought someone to it, and gives a model almost nothing to draw on when it is asked about you.
findings.fix: Either grow the page into something that answers a real question, or fold it into a page that already does.

findings.title: Meta description
findings.summary: No meta description on this page
findings.why: Without one, the snippet under your result is whatever the engine decides to cut out of the page. That is your first impression, chosen by someone else.
findings.fix: Write a 120–155 character description that says what is on this specific page.

findings.title: Canonical link
findings.summary: No canonical link on this page
findings.why: Without a canonical, the same page reached by two URLs can be treated as two pages, splitting whatever weight it has earned.
findings.fix: Add <link rel="canonical" href="..."> pointing at the preferred URL.

findings.title: Language attribute
findings.summary: The <html> element has no lang attribute
findings.why: Screen readers use it to pick a voice and crawlers use it to decide who to show the page to. It is one attribute.
findings.fix: Add lang="en" (or the right language) to the <html> tag.

findings.title: Image alt text
findings.summary: 4 of 4 images have no alt text
findings.why: A crawler reads alt text. An empty alt on a meaningful image removes it from everything a model could learn about you — and removes it from the page entirely for anyone using a screen reader.
findings.fix: Describe the meaningful images. Mark the purely decorative ones alt="" on purpose so the distinction is deliberate.

findings.title: Structured data (JSON-LD)
findings.summary: No JSON-LD structured data on this page
findings.why: Structured data is the one place you get to state plainly what you are, who you are, and what you sell, in a form a machine does not have to guess at. Without it a model is inferring all of that from prose.
findings.fix: Add an Organization or LocalBusiness block on the homepage and Product or Article blocks on the pages that warrant them.

findings.title: Sections out of a sensible order
findings.summary: On /pricing, pricing sits above the section that justifies it (pricing is section 2, features is section 3)
findings.why: The page asks for a decision before it has made the case for one. A reader hitting a price with no context has nothing to weigh it against, so the number reads as expensive by default.
findings.fix: Move pricing below the features or how-it-works section, or put a short summary of what is included directly above the price.

findings.title: No /llms.txt
findings.summary: No /llms.txt found
findings.why: llms.txt is a routing guide for AI agents, not an access-control file -- it points a model at what's actually worth reading on the site instead of leaving it to guess from a sitemap built for search engines.
findings.fix: Add a Markdown file at /llms.txt: an H1 with the site's name, a one-line summary, and links to the pages most worth an agent's attention.
